name: Priya Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and a junior software developer at a tech company sending appointment reminders to dental clinics. I finished a two-year college diploma after the print shop where I worked closed, so I still need a senior to check my code, and I never use AI tools. Dev, my partner, drives a bus; our children are grown, we rent, and our lower wages have left us about three weeks of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the office that small AI shortcuts will not change the appointment reminders we send to dental clinics very much. I still want a person to check the date and patient number before a message goes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58 and only a junior developer, even after my two-year college diploma. Dev’s bus-driving wage and my lower developer pay just cover the rent, and we have three weeks of expenses saved; I worry about any ordinary cut in hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep fixing reminder bugs with the senior developer and ask for a full shift roster each month. We would stop buying takeaway lunches while our savings are below a month of bills, and I would not buy an AI subscription.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious even if AI mostly stalls. Our grown children have homes of their own. A missed shift still shows up in our rent money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you come to coding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worked in a print shop until the presses closed, then took a two-year college diploma. My first code job came late, and I am still the person who asks where a setting is stored.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your children for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not budget for that. They have their own rent and families, and I would rather know early if my hours are changing.

think: I have **three weeks saved** on lower junior pay.
I fear **lost hours** even without a big AI change.

**Stop takeaway lunches** until savings exceed a month of bills.

fieldNote: She entered coding **after print work** and still needs review of junior changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI writing, checking, coding and answering customers could take the simple reminder fixes that juniors get. I would ask the staff association to seek written notice of any hours cuts for all of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the easy tickets disappear, I could be the first person with fewer paid hours. I cannot bridge months without work, and Dev’s bus wage cannot carry the rent and food alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d join the staff association’s group meeting this month to ask for written hours notice. If the company cuts my shifts, I’d search for paid local clinic software support openings only if the wages cover our rent and basic bills; meanwhile we would keep the takeaway cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed about my own hours. The association cannot make a vacancy, but a week of notice is better than hearing at the end of a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the group ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would ask together for a clear list of which reminder jobs stay with people and how much notice comes before reduced shifts. I would not speak for the whole staff on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why clinic support?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know which reminder message causes a patient to turn up on the wrong day. I do not yet know if a clinic nearby would pay enough for us to live on.

I want **paid clinic support** to be a real vacancy, not a promise.

fieldNote: Her **collective request** seeks information and notice, not a guaranteed employer concession.
She treats **clinic support** as a conditional paid opening after reduced hours, with few similar software jobs nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write the reminder code and answer clinic messages for less than our team. Robots doing hands-on bus work arrive about 2031, so Dev’s driving may face a later shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior job to go when the software can do nearly all the thinking work. Three weeks saved would vanish quickly; Dev’s wage may last a few more years, but I cannot pretend it replaces mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the staff association to request a group meeting on written severance and hours notice now. If my job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local reception or clinic-support openings only where vacancies exist and wages cover rent and food; I would also ask the public employment office what support we actually qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed and short of sleep. I can make calls, but I cannot make three weeks of cash last a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why reception when AI answers customers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know those jobs could shrink too. I would only take a real paid opening, and I would not call it a safe career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Dev take more driving shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not ask Dev to add shifts without knowing whether the bus company offers them. Even extra driving hours could change when physical robots arrive around 2031.

I know **three weeks saved** cannot replace my pay.

**Apply for local openings** after 2028 job loss only if vacancies cover rent and food.
**Ask public employment office** what help we qualify for if displaced.

S2.quote: I cannot make three weeks of cash last a year.
fieldNote: Her **2028 code exposure** precedes possible bus robotics around 2031.
She asks about **actual public support** rather than assuming an entitlement, while looking for a wage that covers rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives us a few years to demand a fair changeover, while reminder code still faces the thinking system first. Robots could reach Dev’s bus work about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might keep earning long enough to put a month of rent aside, but our wages leave little spare cash. I still think my junior code job may end by 2031; more warning does not make it safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the staff association to bargain as a group for paid training time and written hours notice, and I’d attend its next meeting. If the company grants paid time, I’d enrol in its clinic records course and practise correcting one anonymized record a week; we would save 40 monthly only while both wages hold, and I’d apply for paid local records openings after 2031 job loss only if vacancies cover rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious, with some time to organise, but still scared of losing my own wage. A month of rent would help me search; it would not buy a new profession.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who pays for the records course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not pay the fee out of our three weeks of savings. I would enrol only if the employer funds the course and lets me attend on paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company says no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the junior job while it exists and ask the association what notice we can get. I would not say I had retrained just because I asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade before full AGI in 2036 gives workers time to bargain for a decent transition. Physical bus robots may come about 2039, three years after the reminder code changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be older and still have no promise that my low-paid junior role lasts until I stop working. Our three-week buffer could grow if both wages continue, but I will not count on a pension amount I have not checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep doing the clinic reminders and ask the staff association each year for a joint review of staffing and paid training. We would save 50 monthly if both wages last; if my developer job ends after 2036, I’d search paid local clinic-record openings only where vacancies and wages cover rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d stay anxious about my own income because the cushion is thin now. A decade gives us meetings and small savings, not a guaranteed landing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at the annual review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask which clinic messages still need a person and how many junior hours are funded. I would want the answer in writing, not a rumour in the corridor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children support you later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope to see them often, but I will not write their income into our rent budget. Dev and I need a plan based on our own pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my junior code wage could end before I can build any savings. Written hours notice, a real paid local clinic vacancy and clear information from the public employment office would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether our grown children could cover the rent. I love our grown children, but I will not build a budget on money they need for their own homes.

headlineQuote: I love our grown children, but I will not build a budget on money they need for their own homes.
portrait: Priya is a **58-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma and lower pay.
She and Dev rent with **three weeks saved**; their grown children have separate homes.
She **never uses AI** and favours group notice and funded paid learning.
She fears **2028 AGI** reaching reminder code before robots reach Dev’s bus around 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her junior wage before savings or paid local work appear.
whatWouldHelp: **Written hours notice**, a paid clinic vacancy and actual public-support information would help.
